parsed_answer.content: In the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), method execution requires linking identifiers in source code to actual memory addresses of machine instructions. This resolution process is broadly split into two distinct paradigms: static binding and dynamic binding. Understanding the dichotomy between these two mechanisms is paramount for writing high-performance, polymorphic code and diagnosing subtle linkage errors during runtime. Static binding, frequently referred to as early binding or compile-time binding, occurs when the compiler possesses complete, unambiguous type information during the compilation phase. Because the exact method declaration or field cannot be overridden or shadowed in a polymorphic manner, the compiler embeds a direct symbolic reference or direct target offset into the generated bytecode constant pool. Conversely, dynamic binding—also known as late binding or runtime binding—is the backbone of Java's runtime polymorphism. When a subclass overrides a method declared in a superclass, the compiler cannot definitively resolve which implementation to execute solely from the reference type at compile-time. Instead, the decision is deferred until execution, relying on the actual runtime type of the object instance heap allocation. This mechanism relies heavily on the JVM's method table (vtable) and interface table (itable) architectures to execute dynamic dispatch efficiently.

items: Static binding is strictly utilized for methods marked as private, static, or final, as well as constructor invocations using 'super' or 'this' via the invokespecial bytecode instruction. Since these entities cannot be overridden by subclasses, the compiler resolves them deterministically.

Method overloading is a prime compile-time phenomenon resolved via static binding. The compiler examines the static declared type of the reference parameters at compile time to select the precise method signature, entirely independent of any runtime casting or subclassing.

Dynamic binding utilizes the invokevirtual and invokeinterface bytecode instructions. When the JVM encounters these, it inspects the object header stored in the heap to locate the class's method table (vtable), resolving the exact method address dynamically.

HotSpot JVM optimizes dynamic binding through inline caches. Instead of traversing the vtable on every single invocation, the JIT compiler caches the last resolved target class, transforming polymorphic dispatches into fast monomorphic guarded checks.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap involves attempting to override static methods. Because static methods are bound statically at compile-time based on the reference type rather than the object instance, writing code that expects polymorphic execution on static methods will fail silently or result in logical bugs. Always ensure that methods requiring polymorphic runtime behavior are non-static instance methods.
